title: Power Passport: Scoring Dead Factories on Amps, Permits
one_liner: A database and paid inspection report that rates shuttered Midwest plants on the things reshoring manufacturers actually need (utility service, slab, crane, transferable air and discharge permits) instead of square footage.
customer: Reshoring manufacturers and their site-selection consultants (first buyer). Industrial listing brokers and sellers of dead factories (they pay to differentiate their listings). Regional economic-development bodies and utility economic-development teams (annual license).
problem: Brokers list buildings by square feet, clear height and dock doors. A reshoring plant needs enough energized 480V/13.2kV capacity, a slab that can carry presses and large CNCs, crane rails, and a transferable Ohio EPA air permit for a paint or wash line. Greenfield permitting and long-lead transformers and switchgear can add 9-18 months before the first good part. Meanwhile data-center developers are hunting the same brownfield shells for their existing utility service, so the buildings that suit manufacturing are disappearing without either side understanding what was in them.
solution: Build a parcel-level dataset of pre-2005 industrial buildings across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Indiana by combining public air and wastewater permit records, county parcel data, utility maps, aerial imagery for crane bays and rail spurs, and Phase I history. Score each building on power, permits, structure and contamination risk. Sell a 'Power Passport': a 12-page report with a licensed industrial electrician's walk-through, gear nameplate photos, permit transferability notes and utility will-serve context, delivered in 5 days.
why_now: The 2026 reshoring wave and the data-center land grab are competing for the same shells. Transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in many months to years. The gap between what manufacturers need and what listings say is at its widest, and brokers have no tooling to fill it.
revenue_model: $1.5k-$3.5k per Passport (paid by the broker or seller, or by the buyer). A 0.5%-1% success fee on closed industrial deals. $25k-$60k per year data licences to economic-development agencies, utilities and site-selection firms. Later, a capital vehicle that buys the best shells and subdivides them into permitted multi-tenant 'factory condos'.
non_obvious_insight: In a dead Ohio plant the building is the cheapest part. The energized service, the paper permits and the crane rails are the asset, and they are invisible to anyone who has not tried to open a factory. Every reshorer I know lost most of a year to power and permits, not to hiring.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (Akron/Canton or the Mahoning Valley). Pull public Ohio EPA permit records and county parcel data to list 150 candidate buildings. Hire an electrician for 20 walk-throughs at about $150 per hour. Cold-call 25 industrial listing brokers offering a free first Passport in exchange for a testimonial and a right to the data. Convert 3-5 into paying $1.5k reports and one economic-development office into a pilot licence.

title: Care-Home Trigger Desk: Evacuate, Shelter, Cool
one_liner: Automatic, pre-contracted action triggers that move older residents before fire, flood or heat-driven power loss becomes lethal.
customer: Multi-site senior living, assisted living and nursing operators in wildfire, coastal and heat-prone states, and their liability insurers.
problem: Older adults dominate heat, fire and hurricane deaths. Federal emergency-preparedness rules require plans but not pre-committed execution: buses, generator fuel, receiving-facility agreements and staff call-ins. Loss of power in heat kills.
solution: A facility-specific trigger sheet tied to near-real-time satellite fire detection, fire-spread modeling, AI weather ensembles and grid outage alerts. It launches staged actions: pre-contracted transport with SLAs, receiving-facility agreements, generator fuel top-ups and cooling-room setup, with an audit trail and drill simulations. Sold per bed per month.
why_now: Near-real-time satellite fire detection is getting funded and commercial (Satellites on Fire raised $2.7M), AI forecasting is cheap, and the summer 2026 heat set off demand for concrete heat plans.
revenue_model: $8-20 per bed per month, transport contract margin and insurer premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not information but pre-committed execution. Care homes have a legal duty and insurer pressure to buy it.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 operators in California and Colorado, build trigger sheets for 20 facilities, and sign transport partners.

title: Voice-Agent Cash-Price Negotiator for Imaging
one_liner: AI voice agents that call 20-30 local facilities, negotiate a guaranteed cash bundle for an MRI, CT or scope, and book it for the newly uninsured.
customer: Uninsured and high-deductible patients (Urban estimates 4.8M newly uninsured after the ACA subsidy expiry; subsidy-cliff self-employed), small employers, and imaging centers, labs and ASCs with idle capacity.
problem: Posted prices are inconsistent and unusable, and cash prices for the same MRI can differ ~10x. Patients will not make 20 phone calls or negotiate, while facilities have idle slots.
solution: The patient submits an order. Agents call and email facilities for real quotes and slot availability, negotiate global-fee prepay bundles, filter for accreditation and quality, return one guaranteed price and book, with escrowed payment.
why_now: Real-time voice agents became reliable in 2025-26, and coverage loss is growing (ACA subsidies expired; Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027). Posted-price marketplaces exist but they don't negotiate dynamically.
revenue_model: $19-39 per booked procedure plus a 5-10% fee from facilities filling otherwise idle slots (cash-pay only, structured to avoid federal-program referral issues).
non_obvious_insight: Cash price is a negotiated market for empty slots. Discovery cost used to be too high per patient, and voice agents make it nearly free.
first_30_days: Concierge 50 MRI, CT and colonoscopy quotes in one metro with call scripts and an LLM voice agent on top. Publish the price spread, sign 5 imaging centers, and charge $29 per booking.

title: Rare Blood Group Assay Foundry
one_liner: Turn each newly recognized blood-group gene into research-use genotyping controls and panels for reference labs, starting with the MAL deletions that define AnWj-negative blood.
customer: Immunohematology reference labs, rare-donor programs and blood centers. Blood-group genotyping platform vendors that want to add content are a second buyer.
problem: AnWj-negative patients, over 99.9% of people are AnWj-positive, can form antibodies against AnWj and risk serious transfusion reactions from ordinary units, and compatible donors are 'extraordinarily difficult' to find. Antibody testing finds the patients but cannot identify rare genetic carriers or donors. Volumes are too small for large diagnostics companies to prioritize.
solution: A small molecular-biology team designs, validates and sells RUO kits: synthetic positive-control DNA for the published MAL deletions, primer and probe sets, and a small validation panel. It then repeats the process for each new ISBT system or rare antigen as the genes are published. It also licenses content to genotyping platform vendors and offers a sample-testing service for rare-donor registries.
why_now: MAL was formally recognized as ISBT blood group system 047 in 2026, and the authors say genotyping tests 'can potentially be incorporated into existing blood group genotyping systems.' Nobody has yet turned the finding into a commercial assay. Cheap gene synthesis and long-read or targeted sequencing make a low-volume, high-value control kit practical for a small team.
revenue_model: RUO control and primer kits at roughly $500-2,000 each, per-sample testing fees for registries, and content-licensing or royalty deals with platform vendors. Later, a CLIA or LDT lab service.
non_obvious_insight: Every new blood-group gene discovery creates a diagnostic gap that big vendors ignore because volume is tiny, and the 47th ISBT system was only just recognized. The NHS Blood and Transplant discovery took nearly 20 years and states that serological testing 'cannot identify rare genetic cases without genetic sequencing' (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260918024828.htm; Blood 2024, DOI 10.1182/blood.2024025099). A repeatable foundry that converts each new ISBT gene into a control kit captures a stream of these gaps. Rare-donor matching is a high-willingness-to-pay niche because a single unmatched patient can cost a hospital far more than a kit.
first_30_days: Design gBlock-style synthetic controls for the MAL deletion alleles reported in the Blood paper and validate them on public or donated DNA. Contact the NHS Blood and Transplant IBGRL, the American Rare Donor Program and 5-10 US and EU reference labs to trial the RUO kit. Line up a second gene from the recent ISBT additions. Pitch two platform vendors on a content deal.

title: Billable Legacy Circles for Advance Care Planning
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare delivery/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Mental health/loneliness/community/meaning
one_liner: Community 'legacy circles' where older adults tell their life stories and finish their advance directives, with a clinician in the room to bill the Medicare advance-care-planning visit.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs chasing advance-care-planning quality measures (paying per completed and documented ACP), plus adults 60+ paying about $79-99 for the circle and a keepsake legacy book.
problem: The longevity industry sells more years but says nothing about what they are for, while the 65+ population is peaking and lonely. Advance care planning has had Medicare billing codes for years (99497/99498), yet few eligible people have one, because it is framed as paperwork about death and clinicians have no time. The meaning conversation people actually want is unbilled, and the billable one is avoided.
solution: A 4-session circle of 6-8 people in libraries, churches and senior centers covers values, life story (dignity-therapy style prompts) and what a good ending looks like. Each participant then has a 30-minute individual ACP visit with an NP or social worker under a billing clinician, who files the health-care proxy or POLST. AI transcription and editing produce a 'legacy book' or short video for family. Plans get documented ACPs and engagement data, and participants get a keepsake and a group of peers.
why_now: About 4M Americans turn 65 each year through 2027, so demand is at a peak. Advantage plans are under margin and Star-rating pressure and want cheap, measurable gap-closing. AI transcription and editing make personalized legacy artifacts cheap. Longevity and GLP-1 hype have surfaced the 'healthspan for what' question.
revenue_model: ACP visit billing (about $85-100 per 99497 under Medicare), per-completion fees from MA plans and ACOs, $79-99 participant fee for the circle and legacy book, and sponsorship by estate-planning and elder-law firms.
non_obvious_insight: Advance care planning fails because it is sold as death admin and done alone. Framed as a legacy-building group with a keepsake, participants pull themselves in. The billing code is the boring spine that lets a community and meaning program be paid by a health plan. The group covers the reflection, and the individual visit, not the group, is what gets billed.
first_30_days: Recruit one NP or LCSW (with a supervising physician) and two host venues, such as a public library and a church. Run three circles at $79 and produce sample legacy books. Take the results to the quality lead of one MA plan or ACO that publishes an ACP gap list. Confirm payer-specific billing rules with a compliance advisor before billing anything.

title: Drug Safety Radar for Pet Medicines
one_liner: A real-world evidence network that reads clinic notes and insurance claims to spot adverse events for newly launched pet drugs and biologics, sold to manufacturers as pharmacovigilance.
customer: Animal-health manufacturers' safety and medical-affairs teams and biotechs launching first-in-class pet therapeutics; later regulators' contractors and insurers.
problem: Adverse-event reporting in vet medicine is voluntary and sparse, and clinics rarely file forms. New launches are arriving on conditional approvals and emergency authorizations, and the post-market evidence burden is growing.
solution: Consent-based feeds from ambient-scribe notes, PIMS and insurer claims. LLMs extract exposures and events, auto-draft FDA-format adverse-event reports in one click for clinics, and run signal detection with matched comparison cohorts. First product: a fixed-fee retrospective signal report for one drug class using one insurer's de-identified claims plus 20-50 clinics.
why_now: FDA has issued 15 emergency authorizations and 3 conditional approvals for screwworm drugs as of 2026-09-03, and Loyal's LOY-002 has cleared two of three technical sections with launch possible before year-end. Ambient scribes turn notes into structured text, and IDEXX/CoVet suggests data will get walled off by incumbents.
revenue_model: $50-250K per drug program per year, per-report fees, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: When launches lean on conditional approvals and emergency authorizations, evidence generation becomes a cost manufacturers must pay, not a nice-to-have. The winning data source is neutral: insurers plus clinics through scribes, not the PIMS vendors who will gate access.
first_30_days: Contact safety and medical-affairs leads at 5 mid-size animal-health companies. Propose a $40K retrospective signal study on a public safety question with an insurer data partner. Release a free one-click adverse-event drafting tool to 20 clinics to seed data.

title: Landing Fund: Sweden's Layoff Council for US Employers
one_liner: Employers pay about 0.3% of payroll into a pooled transition fund that gives every laid-off employee case management, retraining money and bridge pay, so companies can restructure without severance drama.
customer: CFOs and CHROs at 200-3,000-employee US companies (software, fintech, insurance, BPO, media) that are restructuring around AI or expect to. Reached through PEOs, HR brokers and benefits consultants.
problem: US severance is ad hoc (about 12-14 weeks for white-collar staff) and outplacement is usually a webinar. Leaders delay or botch layoffs because there is no humane, pre-agreed answer to 'what happens to the people we cut.' One tracker counts roughly 205,000 AI-attributed US layoffs through August 2026, concentrated in entry-level and back-office roles.
solution: A US version of Sweden's Trygghetsrådet (TRR). Employers join a pool at a set percentage of payroll. When someone is laid off they get a named case manager, retraining vouchers, a 2-4 month bridge-pay top-up, and a COBRA/health bridge subsidy, with providers paid partly on outcomes. Employers get a standard offboarding playbook, smaller bespoke severance, and less litigation and survivor-morale damage. Launch as prepaid 'transition credits' (no insurance license needed) and graduate to a captive or reinsured product.
why_now: AI became the top stated reason for corporate job cuts in the spring of 2026, entry-level white-collar hiring has collapsed, and executives are being publicly punished for how they lay people off. In Sweden the model covers 30,000+ companies and about 700,000 employees on 0.3% of payroll, and roughly 9 in 10 active clients found work, study or self-employment within seven months (2019 figures).
revenue_model: Per-employee-per-month or a percentage of payroll (0.2-0.4%). Unspent reserves fund the next cohort, with margin on training-partner rev share and, later, insurance float.
non_obvious_insight: Sweden's system works because employers fund it collectively, so no single firm carries the full cost of a big layoff, and that pooling turns a dreaded cost into a predictable premium. The buyer's real pain is decision speed and reputation, not the money. A ready-made, respected answer to 'what about the people' lets an executive act faster and more humanely, which is why the product can sell before any regulator asks for it.
first_30_days: Build a 'layoff readiness pack' (offboarding checklist, manager scripts, fund terms) and pitch 15 mid-size companies through two PEOs and an HR consultancy. Line up two training providers and one career-coaching group. Target letters of intent from 5-10 founding employers covering about 5,000 employees at roughly $15 per employee per month, with a first paying pool by month 3.

title: Mindbody Escape Hatch: Studio Migration Concierge
one_liner: A flat-fee service that moves a studio's members, class packs and payment tokens off Mindbody without losing revenue.
customer: Boutique studios, gyms, yoga and Pilates operators on Mindbody (about 40,000 businesses) paying $159-699 per month plus marketplace commissions.
problem: After the ClassPass/Mindbody/EGYM combination (a $7.5B deal completed in 2026), owners report about 23.5 percent effective marketplace commissions and a roughly $500 data-export fee on cancellation. Lock-in is not the software but the card-on-file payment tokens and member history, so owners fear migration will churn members.
solution: A fixed-fee migration ($1.5-3k): export clients, attendance, waivers, packs and memberships; execute PCI-compliant processor-to-processor token migration; map intro offers and unlimited plans; rebuild schedule widgets; run parallel billing checks; and message members by SMS. Target alternative platforms pay a bounty per migrated studio.
why_now: Consolidation gave studios a reason to re-evaluate, ClassPass is rolling out studio-friendly policies in response to complaints, and processors now support token migration.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per migration plus $200-400 bounty per studio from the receiving software vendor and an optional $99 per month retention audit.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is edge-case knowledge (paused members, unlimited plans, refunds, tokens), not software, and rival vendors will pay you for customers because their own acquisition cost is high.
first_30_days: Offer five free migration audits in studio-owner communities, pick two target platforms, run three at-cost pilot migrations, and turn the playbook into a checklist and pricing page.

title: Install Clubs: Brazilian Consórcio for Home Contractors
one_liner: A contractor-anchored, interest-free buying pool: 60-200 homeowners pay monthly into escrow and each month a few move up the queue (by draw or bid) to get their roof, heat pump or solar+battery installed.
customer: Independent home-service contractors (roofing, HVAC/heat pump, solar+storage, windows) with 5-50 staff who want pre-sold backlog. Their end users are homeowners who have been quoted $8-20k and don't want a 9-12% HELOC or home-improvement loan.
problem: Big-ticket home upgrades stall on financing. Contractors burn 10-20% of revenue on lead gen and lose many quoted jobs because the homeowner can't or won't borrow. The 25C/25D federal credits ended for installs after Dec 31, 2025, so the effective price jumped overnight.
solution: Software + bank escrow + a lawyer-drafted prepaid-service template that lets a contractor run a 'club' for one product (e.g., a $9k heat-pump install). Members pay $100-200/month into segregated escrow. Every month one or more members are allocated an install by lottery or by bidding extra to jump the queue. The contractor is the counterparty and delivers at a locked price, so there is no loan and no interest. The platform earns an administration fee instead of interest, as Brazilian consórcios do.
why_now: Brazil's consórcio system hit a record 12.76M active participants and about R$500B of credit sold in 2025, in a high-rate environment, so the model is proven when loans are expensive. In the US the 25C/25D credits vanished on Dec 31, 2025, rates are still high, and the only consórcio-style player I found (NWX) sells general credit letters for real estate and vehicles. Nobody has wrapped the pool around a service the seller delivers.
revenue_model: Administration fee of roughly 8-12% of contract value collected in monthly installments, a SaaS fee per contractor club, and a share of escrow float yield.
non_obvious_insight: A consórcio is not a loan, it is a queue with a price guarantee. Making the licensed contractor the counterparty turns the pool into a prepaid-service escrow (like layaway) instead of a credit product, which sidesteps most lending regulation. The contractor gets what it wants most: scheduled backlog, cash before work, and near-zero CAC because 'your neighbor's roof gets done this month' recruits the next member. Homeowners who were declined or scared off by loans are the fastest-filling segment.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 contractors in one state. Get an escrow account at a community bank and a prepaid-service agreement drafted by a lawyer who knows that state's home-improvement deposit rules. Mine each contractor's list of past quotes that never closed and pre-enroll about 40 members in a 'Founders Club' at about $150/month for a $9k install. Run the first allocation in month 2, so the first installed job and first admin-fee revenue land by around day 60.

title: Part-Time Retired Journeymen as Apprentice Supervisors
one_liner: Supervision-as-a-service: retired licensed tradespeople work 2-3 days a week as the supervising journeyman that lets small shops deploy the apprentices and helpers they already have.
customer: 5-25 employee electrical, plumbing and HVAC shops with unlicensed helpers or apprentices, starting in one state with clear ratio and qualifier rules. They pay by the hour.
problem: The headlines say the pipeline is the shortage, but the Gen Z enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage. For many shops the binding constraint is licensed supervision, because ratio rules cap helpers per journeyman. Data-center overtime ($130-170K for journeymen, vendor stat) pulls supervisors off residential work. ABC says most of the 349K 2026 shortfall is retirements, yet retirees hold exactly the scarce credential and are unused.
solution: A vetted, insured bench of retired journeymen and masters placed part-time in shops as supervising journeyman and mentor. The platform verifies licenses, runs employer-of-record or 1099 structure per state rules, handles workers' comp, and automates the apprenticeship hour logs boards require. Shops book blocks such as Tue-Thu 7-3.
why_now: ABC's 2026 gap of 349K is mostly retirement. Data centers now account for nearly a third of the shortage. Immigration enforcement removes helpers, so shops need to hire and supervise local apprentices fast. Trade-school hype is masking a thin pipeline.
revenue_model: Shops pay about $75-110 per hour billed. The platform keeps 20-25% and the retiree keeps the rest. Add $150-250 per month for hour-logging and compliance software.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not labor, it is supervision minutes, and retirees want 16-hour weeks that no normal employer offers. A supervising journeyman unlocks one or two helpers billing at journeyman-adjacent rates, so shops can pay a premium and still gain margin. Rules vary by state and must be verified before launch.
first_30_days: Pick one trade (electrical) in one state with clear ratio rules. Recruit 15 retirees from union retiree groups and lapsing-license lists. Sign 5 shops with 3+ helpers who are idle or under-deployed. Bill the first hours in week 3.

title: Shift-Matched Nurse Households Near Hospitals
angle: Pairing 2: Real estate (master leases in concession-heavy buildings) x Single-parent childcare and affordability
one_liner: Master-lease three- and four-bedroom units near hospitals and match two single-parent nurses with interlocking shifts and similar-aged kids into one household, so overnight and early-morning care is built into the lease. The hospital pays for placement.
customer: Hospitals and health systems (per-placement or per-retained-nurse fee from recruitment and retention budgets), landlords in lease-up (guaranteed master-lease rent), and nurses (their half of rent).
problem: Single parents spend about 35% of income on childcare and the licensed system barely operates at night or on rotating schedules. Nurses' 12-hour rotating shifts do not fit center hours. Turnover of a bedside RN costs a hospital roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile large units near hospitals sit vacant behind concessions, and middle-income renters' late payments rose from 14.3% to 21.6% in a year.
solution: The platform (backed by the hospital's guarantee) master-leases large units from landlords for 12-24 months, then matches nurses on compatible shift patterns, school zone and child ages, with background checks, a shared household agreement, and an optional paid caregiver pool for overlap gaps. Each household pays about half the rent it would pay alone and has an adult at home when the other is at work. Students, residents and travel nurses can fill spare rooms.
why_now: Concessions of 15-37% and 7% vacancy make landlords eager for a guaranteed 12-24 month lease with a hospital-backed credit. Hospitals face the weakest cost position in years (Medicaid work requirements from Jan 2027 hit margins of expansion-state hospitals) and cannot afford travel-nurse premiums. Childcare costs are the top named barrier for early-career nurses.
revenue_model: Hospital fee per placed household (about $300-500 a month, justified by retention), plus a 10-15% spread on master-lease rent and caregiver-payroll fees.
non_obvious_insight: Matching on shift patterns is an algorithmic problem no housing platform solves: two nurses on opposite shifts convert the biggest cost in a household (childcare) into an internal schedule, and a hospital's guarantee turns a risky sublease into a credit-enhanced master lease that landlords will happily take at a discount.
first_30_days: Sign a pilot with one hospital's recruitment team and two landlords near campus. Master-lease two 3BR units and recruit four nurse parents from unit-level staffing forums. Write a household agreement and a safety-screening protocol with a family lawyer. Measure retention and shift coverage at 6 months.

title: Half-Plate GLP-1 Menus for Independent Restaurants
one_liner: A menu-engineering kit that converts an independent restaurant's existing dishes into protein-first half-plates priced at about 65-75% of the full plate, to capture GLP-1 households that eat out smaller but still eat out.
customer: Independent and regional restaurants (10-60 seats, $1-4M revenue) in metros with a high share of higher-income Gen X and Boomer diners, paying $499 setup plus $99-149/month.
problem: Circana estimates 23% of US households now include a GLP-1 user and that these users will account for about 35% of food and beverage sales by 2030. Those households cut traditional retail food and beverage purchases, especially high-carb, high-sugar, refrigerated and frozen items, and shift toward protein, fiber, fresh produce and restaurant spending, yet they still outspend non-users. Big chains are chasing this, but independents have no menu-engineering staff. If they simply shrink portions at the same price, GLP-1 customers feel ripped off. If they shrink and cut the price proportionally, margins collapse.
solution: For each restaurant, a done-for-you overlay: 4-6 existing dishes re-specified as half-plates with protein grams, plate-cost and margin tables, pricing at 65-75% of full price to protect gross margin per cover, a small-plate 'protein first' section, and a nausea-friendly option (low-fat, low-volume). Deliverables include a printable menu insert, a QR page, POS/online-ordering item entries (Toast, Square, Clover) and simple local marketing via medspas, GLP-1 telehealth clinics and pharmacies that hand out a 'restaurants near you that fit your plan' card. Protein numbers come from recipe-level calculations, not vague 'healthy' badges.
why_now: GLP-1 adoption is at household scale (Circana, November 2025), and oral versions (Wegovy pill December 2025, Foundayo April 2026) plus cash prices as low as $149-$299/month on TrumpRx.gov are pulling in more users. Novo Nordisk is cutting list prices to $675/month in January 2027. Meanwhile restaurant spending is recovering, with independents beating national chains and Gen Z leading (BofA, August 2026), so independent owners are looking for a differentiator national brands cannot copy quickly.
revenue_model: $499 one-time setup, $99-149/month for menu updates, QR/landing page and local partnership marketing. Optional performance share (for example, $1 per redeemed 'plan card'). Later: bulk licensing to regional chains and food-service distributors.
non_obvious_insight: The obvious read is 'GLP-1 kills food demand'. The data says something different: users cut retail food but restaurant spending rises and total spend still exceeds non-users, so the demand shifts channel and portion size rather than disappearing. The winner is margin engineering (a half-plate that keeps dollars per cover), not a health-halo badge. Evidence: Circana (Nov 18, 2025) https://www.circana.com/post/glp-1-medication-users-to-represent-35-percent-of-u-s-food-and-beverage-sales-by-2030 and https://www.circana.com/insights-hub/glp-1s-consumer-behavior (23% of households, 35% by 2030, restaurants up, retail food down, users skew Gen X with income over $100K). Independents outperform chains: https://institute.bankofamerica.com/economic-insights/restaurants-and-discretionary-spending.html . Caveat: the Circana pages I could read did not give the size of the restaurant-spend lift, so validate it with a few owners' POS data.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Walk in on 20 independent restaurants with a one-page free audit of their own top 5 dishes (protein grams, half-plate cost and price). Convert 5-8 into paid setups. In parallel, sign 2-3 medspas or pharmacies to hand out the plan card and track redemptions to build a case study. Target: 5 paying restaurants and one measurable uplift story (covers or check average on half-plates) by day 30.

title: Hour-Meter Forensics for Used Farm Equipment
angle: Pairing 2: Food & agriculture x Cybersecurity/deepfake fraud/identity verification/scams
one_liner: An independent inspection and identity report for used tractors and combines that cross-checks engine-hour logs across ECUs, serial numbers and liens to catch rolled-back hours and phantom sellers.
customer: Used-equipment dealers and auction houses, equipment-finance lenders and Farm Credit associations, and farmers buying $100K-800K machines on classifieds and marketplaces.
problem: Used machine value is driven by hours. Tools that roll back hour meters and ECU logs are openly sold, and buyers wire deposits to fake sellers. Lien and ownership checks are patchy. Row crops are projected to lose money for a fourth straight year and farm bankruptcies are up 19%, so lenders care about collateral and farmers buy used. Historically independent shops could not read OEM diagnostics, so no neutral party could verify a machine's history.
solution: Mobile mechanics with OEM-capable diagnostic tools pull hour counts from every module (engine, transmission, monitor, telematics) and compare them, review calibration and replacement logs, and flag mismatches. An identity module checks the serial against photos, runs a UCC lien search and does seller KYC, with escrow released on inspection. Output is a signed 'Hours Verified' certificate, later an API for lenders and auction platforms.
why_now: Deere's $99M settlement obliges it to open its diagnostic and repair tools for 10 years, creating independent access to the machine's real history for the first time. Repair restrictions cost farmers about $4.2B a year. Squeezed farm incomes push demand toward used machines, and leaked ID data feeds synthetic seller identities.
revenue_model: $195-495 per inspection paid by buyer or lender, $99 per lot from auction houses, a 0.5-1% escrow fee, and per-collateral fees from lenders for portfolio audits.
non_obvious_insight: Right-to-repair created a security market. Once independent shops can read what a machine really did, its history becomes a verifiable identity, a Carfax-like asset that OEM dealers, who profit from service and trade-ins, are structurally reluctant to publish. Whoever publishes trusted hours first owns the data asset.
first_30_days: Hire two ag mechanics who already own diagnostic tools. Offer a $150 'Hours Check' at three auction houses and five independent dealers during fall auction season. Publish the discrepancy rate as a case study. Then pitch equipment-finance lenders and Farm Credit associations a free 30-machine collateral audit.

title: Grid-Code Commissioning for AI Campuses
one_liner: A test-and-certify service that validates how an AI campus behaves toward the grid (ride-through, load swings, oscillations), produces the field data transmission owners now must demand, and signs off on it.
customer: Owners of 50-500 MW computational-load sites (neoclouds, colo developers, hyperscalers' second-tier builds) that must satisfy a transmission owner's new commissioning process. Secondary: commissioning agents lacking grid-side capability who subcontract the work, and utilities that want a standard test-and-model package to accept.
problem: Traditional commissioning tests the facility against its own failures: pull the utility feed, gensets pick up, resistive load banks hold steady load. It does not test how UPS systems, rectifiers and GPU power supplies respond to voltage sags and frequency dips, or how synchronized training-job power swings interact with the grid. In July 2024 about 1,500 MW of data center load in Virginia dropped off in seconds. NERC's May 2026 Level 3 alert now calls for detailed load modeling, annual stability studies and a commissioning process for computational loads. Transmission owners have nothing to point at, owners have no test protocol, and everyone is using generic vendor models.
solution: A hardware-agnostic test package. Rent existing programmable AI-load emulators (Vertiv, PowerLoad and other liquid-cooled GPU-emulating load banks already exist), add high-speed PMU and power-quality recorders, and run a standard protocol: voltage and frequency ride-through, ramp and step-load profiles from real training traces, oscillation checks, and backup-transfer behavior under dynamic load. Deliver a PE-stamped report and an EMT/PSS/E model-validation dataset shaped for the transmission owner's interconnection group. Offer the same protocol to utilities as a certificate template. The value is the protocol, the sign-off and the model validation, not the hardware.
why_now: NERC issued a Level 3 Alert on May 4, 2026. FERC ordered NERC to file mandatory reliability standards for computational loads by Dec 31, 2026. Texas's SB 6 large-load rule is also expected by year end. The emulator hardware finally exists, but the commissioning process and accepted evidence package do not. The first owners to energize in late 2026 and 2027 will need this or wait months for the utility to sign off.
revenue_model: $150K-400K fixed fee per site (test campaign, report, model validation). $30K-80K per additional hall. Subcontract margin when working under Cx agents. Annual re-test and monitoring subscription of $40K-100K per site. Later, licensing of the protocol to utilities.
non_obvious_insight: Commissioning teams are excellent at proving the facility survives a grid failure and almost blind to proving the grid survives the facility. The IST script stops at the fence line. The utility's planners are working from datasheet models that nobody has ever field-validated, and the person best placed to bridge the two (a data center Cx lead who has run a hundred pull-the-plug tests) has never talked to a transmission planner.
first_30_days: Hire or partner with 2 power-systems engineers (an EMT/protection specialist and a load-bank/field-test lead). Write a public 'reading the NERC Level 3 alert as a commissioning test plan' whitepaper. Pitch 5 commissioning agents on white-label subcontract. Line up an emulator rental partner. Offer a discounted pilot to a 20-50 MW neocloud or colo site heading for energization in the next 6 months, priced at cost in exchange for a published (anonymized) case study and a transmission owner introduction.

title: Robot Pack-Opening with Chain-of-Custody
one_liner: A neutral facility and machine that opens sealed trading-card packs on camera without human hands, sorts hits and ships them, so buyers can trust a break.
customer: Live-stream breakers and repack sellers, game stores running mail-in breaks, and buyers who pay for the 'bot-opened' badge.
problem: Fraud in streamed breaks includes resealed packs with hits removed, counterfeits and non-delivery. Whatnot did about $8B in 2025 and is under litigation, X-ray pack scanning is sold to collectors, and breakers spend heavy labor opening thousands of packs.
solution: A semi-automated cell (slitter, camera, card ID, sleeving) with serial-logged tamper-evident intake seals, a public feed with an audit trail, and a badge. Start as a neutral facility with humans in the loop, opening product breakers ship in, then lease the machine to large breakers.
why_now: Vision-language robot control matured in 2025-26. Litigation and fraud make trust monetizable, and the 2026 robbery wave favors a secured central facility over home streaming setups.
revenue_model: $0.40-1.00 per pack opened, per-hit shipping fees, badge subscriptions and machine leasing.
non_obvious_insight: Trust in breaks is a chain-of-custody problem, not a reputation problem. A machine has no motive to skim hits. Labor arbitrage pays for the machine while trust earns the price premium.
first_30_days: Rent a small secure space and run hands-off, sealed-bag-intake openings for 5 breakers with two part-timers and a phone rig. Charge per pack and prototype the cutter with an off-the-shelf arm.

title: Chargeback Guarantee for Agent-Placed Orders
angle: Pairing 1: AI agents & agent economy x Finance
one_liner: A merchant-side gateway that checks the shopper's signed mandate against the cart, keeps a tamper-proof decision record, and reimburses chargebacks on approved agent orders.
customer: Shopify, BigCommerce and headless merchants doing $5M-$100M GMV that have switched on agentic checkout (ACP, UCP, AP2) and whose acquirers watch their dispute ratios.
problem: Fraud engines score human signals (device, mouse, session) that agents lack, so agent orders are either falsely declined or approved blind. Disputes have no rulebook: neither Visa nor Mastercard has a binding chargeback rule for agent-initiated purchases, the record shows only merchant, timestamp and amount, and Visa's dispute threshold tightened from 2.2% to 1.5% on 2026-04-01. Merchants also have to support ACP, UCP, AP2, MPP and x402 separately.
solution: One integration that accepts all five protocols. It cryptographically verifies the user-signed mandate (spend cap, item constraints, expiry, agent identity) against what was actually ordered, stores an immutable decision record, and auto-builds representment packets. Orders that pass are guaranteed: we pay the chargeback and the fee. Underwriting rests on mandate-versus-cart match, not on behavioral fingerprinting.
why_now: The protocols went live in the last 8 months (MPP 2026-03-18, plus ACP, UCP, AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent). Agent usage is about 62% at comparison but only about 23% at checkout, so trust is the bottleneck. The Ninth Circuit's 2026-08-04 Comet ruling treats the agent as the user, and there is still no fault rulebook from the networks.
revenue_model: 0.5-1.0% of guaranteed agent-order GMV plus $299-1,999 per month gateway SaaS. The guarantee reserve is backed by a $1-2M capital line or a quota-share reinsurer. Loss data can later be licensed to insurers and networks.
non_obvious_insight: Incumbent fraud models are trained on human behavior, so agent traffic is behaviorally blank. The right signal is the mandate, not the session. Whoever holds the mandate-versus-cart record and the loss outcomes becomes the arbiter that networks, acquirers and insurers will need, and that same data is the missing underwriting telemetry for agent risk generally. Merchants will not want to pick among five protocols, so the guarantee is the wedge for owning the plumbing.
first_30_days: Ship a Shopify app in shadow mode for 15-20 merchants: tag agent-origin orders (agent referrers, ACP/UCP headers), log mandates, and back-test which orders would have been disputed. Offer the first 5 merchants a 90-day guarantee capped at $50k each, funded by founder capital plus a small MGA or reinsurer line, at about 0.75% of agent GMV. Publish the observed dispute rates as the pricing basis.

title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.

title: Batteries That Pay Off Utility Arrears
one_liner: Install free home batteries in households behind on bills and let capacity payments retire the debt, which is cheaper for the utility than writing it off.
customer: Utilities, co-ops and munis in high-capacity-price regions (PJM first) that run arrears and shutoff programs. State PUCs and community action agencies co-sponsor. The utility pays from bad-debt and program budgets.
problem: 13.4M households were disconnected in 2024 and about 1 in 6 are behind on bills. Rates rose 7.3% in a year and this is a midterm issue. At the $325/MW-day cap, each kW of dispatchable capacity is worth about $118 a year, so a 5 kW home battery is worth roughly $590 a year gross, before accreditation haircuts and the aggregator's share.
solution: A no-cost 10 kWh 'bill-relief battery' for arrears households, enrolled in a utility or aggregator capacity program. Capacity and energy revenue is credited against the arrears balance for 5-7 years, after which the customer keeps it or the utility retains it. The company handles installation, financing and dispatch. The utility gets less bad debt and fewer politically toxic shutoffs.
why_now: Capacity prices hit the cap, packs cost about $70/kWh, dispatch at scale is proven, and utilities are under political pressure on affordability with few tools.
revenue_model: Per-install fee, a share of capacity revenue while the arrears are being retired, utility program payments, and project finance spread.
non_obvious_insight: At this capacity price, a battery earns more than it costs to give one away. Utility bad debt is a hidden capex budget that has never been spent on assets.
first_30_days: Get one utility's arrears distribution and model unit economics under current capacity prices. Pitch five community action agencies and three co-ops or munis on a 50-home pilot funded by weatherization-adjacent money. Line up a philanthropic first-loss guarantee.

title: Pay-on-Green: Escrow Released by Executable Tests
one_liner: Escrow for agent-to-agent work where the negotiated object is a hashed acceptance test, and money moves only when the test passes.
customer: Growth, data and ops teams at 20-500 person companies that subcontract bulk deliverables (data enrichment, scraping, code migrations, translation with QA) to other vendors' agents, plus the small agent vendors who want guaranteed payment.
problem: Card chargebacks do not fit machine-speed commerce and stablecoin payments are irreversible. The dispute in agent work is almost always 'was it good enough?', and no human can review thousands of small deliverables. The 2026 payment protocols (AP2, ACP, x402, MPP) settle payment but say little about quality or delayed fulfilment.
solution: A 'test-as-contract' escrow. Before work starts, buyer and seller agents agree on an executable acceptance suite: schema and checksum checks, unit tests, planted canary items with known answers, and a rubric graded by a panel of three different-model judges with pre-committed prompts. Funds lock in escrow. On delivery the suite runs in a sandbox and releases funds item by item (partial settlement). Disputes narrow to 'was the test fair?' and go to a small-claims panel with human appeal. Third parties publish reusable verifier suites and earn a royalty per run.
why_now: Agents in 2026 routinely delegate subtasks to other vendors' agents. LLM-as-judge and cheap sandboxes are mature. Four competing payment protocols now exist, and academic proposals for refundable, delayed-fulfilment settlement (for example the Agentic Settlement Protocol paper of September 2026) show the dispute layer is an acknowledged gap.
revenue_model: 1.5-3% escrow fee on GMV, plus $0.01-0.05 per verifier run, plus a royalty share to verifier authors. Enterprise plan with SLAs and private test libraries.
non_obvious_insight: Move the dispute before the money moves. Agents will not argue price, they will argue the test, so the durable asset is a growing library of standard acceptance suites, which works like an ISO standard for agent deliverables. Planted canaries (honeypot items, as crowdsourcing platforms use) catch lazy or fraudulent sellers cheaply.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical where canaries are easy: bulk lead-list verification and web-data extraction. Recruit 5 small agent vendors and 3 buyers from indie-hacker and MCP developer communities. Run escrow manually on Stripe Connect with delayed payouts. Publish 20 open-source acceptance-test templates as lead magnets. Charge 3% and aim for $10k of escrowed GMV.

title: Hospice for Dying Congregations
one_liner: A managed 'final season' service for congregations that are closing, covering the closing liturgy, an oral-history archive, member placement and a community-first sale of the building.
customer: Denominational regional bodies (dioceses, presbyteries, conferences) and individual congregations with fewer than 50 members deciding to close, and community land trusts and developers who want to reuse their buildings.
problem: Lifeway reported 4,000 Protestant closures against 3,800 openings in 2024, and shrinking, aging congregations keep sliding toward closure. The process is legally messy (deeds, endowments, cemeteries, records, sacred objects) and emotionally painful, and it usually ends in a rushed sale to whoever pays most, with members scattering and often falling out of community altogether.
solution: A 6-12 month managed process: a closing service designed with celebrants, a professional oral-history and photo archive digitised for the community, guided placement of members into neighbouring congregations or community groups, and stewardship of stained glass, organs and memorial gifts. We run a request-for-proposals that favours reuse (housing, community centres) under a mission covenant.
why_now: Post-COVID closures never fully rebounded, clergy are aging, and denominations are sitting on stranded property. California's 2023 law allowing affordable housing on faith-owned land, and the copycat 'YIGBY' bills in other states, make community reuse financially viable.
revenue_model: A fixed fee of roughly $15-40k per congregation paid by the denomination or from sale proceeds, plus a 1-3% success fee on community-reuse sales. Optional licensing of archives to historians, genealogists and local libraries.
non_obvious_insight: Dying congregations do not lack real-estate brokers; they lack a good funeral and a dignified narrative. That is the real barrier to a good sale, because grieving members block anything that feels like betrayal. Whoever holds the funeral earns the trust to shape the outcome toward community use, so you sell a good death and earn the property fee as a consequence.
first_30_days: List 20 congregations flagged for closure in a single denomination region. Offer three subsidised 'Last Sunday' packages at about $5k each, and use the outcomes to pitch the regional executive on a standing contract.
